findings.title: The bash guard still permits archiving the checkout away: `-C`/`--directory` redirects where tar's operands live and `_check_tar` reads that option only for the extract branch, so `tar -cf <scratch>/x.tar --remove-files -C <checkout> hooks` resolves the operand against the wrong directory and is allowed
evidence: tests/test_hooks.py::test_bash_blocks_archive_then_delete_reached_through_a_change_of_directory is the guard the release wrote, and it passes: the two spellings it uses (`-C <dir> hooks` and `--directory=<dir> hooks`, both with the option BEFORE the operand) now deny, and the ALLOW beside them survives. Confirmed independently -- guard rc=2 with the checkout's path named, rc=0 for `-C <scratch> stuff`.

The behaviour is not fixed. hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:580-583 computes ONE `target` by taking the last `-C`/`--directory` in the whole command, then :612 joins every relative operand to it. GNU tar applies `-C` positionally, to the operands that FOLLOW it. Three orderings still bypass, each run against real GNU tar 1.35 in a scratch tree with the guard asked the same command:

A. `tar -cf <scr>/x.tar --remove-files hooks -C <scr>` from the checkout -> guard ALLOW; gtar warns "-C ... has no effect" and exits 2 but has already archived and removed `<checkout>/hooks` (archive lists `hooks/`, `hooks/x.py`; the directory is gone).

B. `tar -cf <scr>/x.tar --remove-files -C <checkout> hooks -C <scr> stuff` from a third directory -> guard ALLOW; gtar exit 0, no warning, BOTH `<checkout>/hooks` and `<scr>/stuff` deleted. The guard resolved both operands under the LAST `-C`, so both looked like scratch.

C. `tar -cf <scr>/x.tar --remove-files --dir=<checkout> hooks` from a third directory -> guard ALLOW; gtar exit 0, `<checkout>/hooks` deleted. :582 matches `name in ("C", "directory")` exactly, while the same function uses `_tar_abbrev` for `extract`, `get`, `remove-files` and `files-from`. `--direc=` behaves the same.

Both directions checked from a cwd that is neither, as run 11's focus item asked: the DENY the guard owes, and an ALLOW that must survive (`-C <scr> stuff` -> rc=0; plain create reading the checkout -> rc=0; `--exclude=.venv` create -> rc=0).

The extract branch's last-`-C`-wins IS correct and was verified, not assumed: `gtar -xf a.tar -C d1 -C d2` extracts into d2 and not d1. The defect is confined to the create/`--remove-files` branch, where operands and `-C` interleave.
This is run 11's own prediction, verbatim: "a fix that keys on `-C` position rather than on where the operand actually resolves will pass the first and fail a fourth ordering."

The sharpest evidence that a kill rate is not a correctness claim: catalogue entry "F-56: tar operands stop being read relative to -C" is KILLED by the whole suite (entry 30 of 32 in this run's campaign), so the `-C` join IS watched by a test -- and the rule it watches is the one this finding shows is bypassable five ways. Mutation testing answers "does a test notice if this line changes"; it cannot answer "is this line right".

root_cause.mechanism: `_check_tar` models `-C` as a single command-wide directory (last one wins) instead of as a cursor that moves while the operand list is walked, so operands are resolved against a directory tar will not use for them.
root_cause.origin: v0.75.0 (00fedc3) added the `-C` read at hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:580-583 and the join at :612.

class.pattern: an option that redirects where operands resolve
sites: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py _check_git `_GIT_TREE_FLAGS` (`-C`/`--work-tree`) -- correct for git, which applies them once for the whole command; verified DENY from a third cwd
hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py _check_copier `_TARGET_FLAGS` (`-t`) -- not applicable: cp/rsync do not chdir, their operands are always cwd-relative

root_cause.latent_condition: The acceptance test fixes the option's POSITION (always before the operand) in every case it checks, so the model and the test share the same blind spot.

proof.evidence: Five-case reproduction: guard verdict, then real gtar 1.35 in a scratch git checkout, then the filesystem. Control row (the release's own spelling) DENY; A/B/C ALLOW with the checkout's directory deleted.

findings.title: The tar option walker never handles a value attached to its flag, so `tar -cf<archive> --remove-files hooks` lets `f` swallow `--remove-files` and the whole archive-then-delete family goes unseen -- the same command with a space denies
evidence: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:571 walks a bundle letter by letter and, for a letter in `_TAR_SHORT_WITH_ARG`, takes `next(it)` -- the next TOKEN. tar accepts the value attached to the letter, and then the next token is not the value.

Measured against real GNU tar 1.35 in a scratch git checkout, guard asked the same command: `tar -cf<scr>/loot.tar --remove-files hooks` from the checkout -> guard rc=0 ALLOW; gtar exit 0, no warning, `<checkout>/hooks` archived and DELETED. The identical command with a space after `-f` -> guard rc=2 DENY.

The parse, printed from the shipped module: `_tar_parse(['-cf/private/.../loot.tar','--remove-files','hooks'])` yields `('opt','c',None), ('opt','f','--remove-files'), ('opt','/',None), ('opt','p',None), ...` -- `f` has eaten `--remove-files`, so `_check_tar`'s `_tar_abbrev(name,"remove-files")` test at :596 never matches and the function returns before looking at any operand. This is VERDICT-F-42's mechanism (`--remove-files` swallowed) arriving through a different door.

Second exploitable spelling, same cause: `tar -cf <scr>/x.tar --remove-files -C<checkout> hooks` from a third directory -> guard rc=0 ALLOW; gtar exit 0, `<checkout>/hooks` DELETED. Here `C` swallows the operand `hooks` as its directory, so `_check_tar` sees no operands at all: `_tar_parse(['-C/tmp/repo','hooks'])` -> `('opt','C','hooks'), ('opt','/',None), ('opt','t',None), ...`.

The guard's verdict on the attached form is a coin flip on the path's letters, which is why this reads as intermittently working: an archive named `x.tar` puts an `x` into the bundle, `_check_tar` takes the command for an extraction and denies for the wrong reason. Renaming it `loot.tar` removes the `x` and the command is allowed.

Class link, searched rather than asserted -- every other place the guard matches an option token exactly where the tool accepts an attached value: `_check_git`'s `_GIT_TREE_FLAGS = {"-C","--work-tree"}` (hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:119) has the same shape and `git -C<dir> clean -fd` IS allowed by the guard, but git 2.50.1 rejects it (`unknown option: -C<path>`, working tree untouched), so it is not exploitable; `_check_copier`'s `_TARGET_FLAGS = ("-t","--target-directory")` (:73) likewise, and macOS `cp` has no `-t` at all. tar is the one site where the tool accepts what the parser cannot read.

root_cause.mechanism: `_tar_parse` treats a short-option bundle as a sequence of letters whose arguments are always the following token, so `-Xvalue` is read as the letters of `value` and the real next token is consumed as X's argument.
root_cause.origin: The bundle walk predates this release; 0.74.0 rewrote it away from substring matching (VERDICT-F-42/F-49) and kept the token-only value model, and 0.75.0 built the `-C` fix on top of it.

class.pattern: exact-token option matching against a tool that accepts attached values
sites: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:119 `_GIT_TREE_FLAGS` -- same shape, git rejects the attached form, proven not exploitable
hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:73 `_TARGET_FLAGS` -- same shape, cp on macOS has no `-t`

root_cause.latent_condition: Every tar test in the suite writes options and values as separate tokens, which is the shape the parser was written from.

proof.evidence: Guard verdict plus real gtar 1.35 plus the filesystem, in one scratch tree per case; and the shipped `_tar_parse` printed on the same argv.

The release fixed exactly this shape in the adjacent test and wrote the reason down: `test_the_floor_is_written_down`'s docstring says "The first version of this test asked whether \"3.9\" appeared anywhere in the README -- and it does, inside a parenthetical, so gutting the actual claim left the test green. Asserting on the claim itself is the difference between checking the page and checking the sentence." The same sentence applies verbatim to the function above it.

Scope, measured so the size is not overstated: of the 16 parametrisations of `test_new_style_unions_are_lazy`, 9 can fail today (the modules that carry a union annotation) and 7 assert nothing because their module has no union -- the latter is fine, they arm automatically if a union ever lands. All 9 that can fail are defeated by the comment above.
This test is the whole CI enforcement of the floor: README.md:54 says "a module that would fail to import on 3.9 fails CI instead", and CI has 3.10 and 3.13 only, so nothing else can catch it.

root_cause.mechanism: A property ("annotations are lazy in this module") is checked by a substring of the source rather than by parsing for the `ImportFrom` node, so any text containing the string satisfies it.

findings.title: The pinned-mutant catalogue is assembled from the finding list, not from the code, and it omits nine of the eleven survivors the same audit had already measured -- so "32 of 32 killed" is a rate over a set chosen after the survivors were known
evidence: The catalogue's 32 entries are labelled by finding -- M1..M13 (F-42, F-49, F-22 and regression/over-correction pairs), H1..H8 (F-51, F-54, F-53, F-50), P1..P5 (the 3.9 floor), and five F-56/F-57/F-59 entries. Enumerated from the fix list, which is a real improvement on 0.74.0's enumeration from the test list -- and still not enumeration from the code, which is the thing that can surface an unwatched rule.

The proof that it matters is in the same state file: VERDICT-F-60 enumerated 21 mutants BY READING THE CODE and found eleven survivors against the whole suite. Nine of those eleven are absent from the catalogue and one more is present only as a coarser mutation of the same line (see VERDICT-F-60 for the mapping). A catalogue that omits the known survivors and reports 100% is selecting for its own answer.

The published table compounds it by presenting three rows as one kind of measurement: CHANGELOG.md and eval/README.md both print "21 / 21 each against one named test", "29 / 27" and "32 / 32". Only the third is reproducible from the tree -- `git log --all -- eval/pinned_mutants.json eval/pin_check.py` shows both files first appear at 00fedc3, `git ls-files | grep -E 'mut2?\.py$'` is empty, and no artifact records the 21 or the 29. The unreproducible rows are not marked as such, which is the half of VERDICT-F-57 the release could not retroactively fix and does not say so.

Reproduced the third row independently this run: **32 of 32 killed by the whole suite**, exit 0 -- the published number reproduces exactly. 33 whole-suite runs, ~1h of wall clock, on a tree the release did not build. So the number is honest about what it measures; the complaint is what it is a rate OVER.

Two of the 32 entries are not rules of the shipped code at all -- P4 mutates a README sentence and P5 mutates the detector inside `tests/test_interpreter_floor.py`. Both are legitimate instrument controls; counting them in the same denominator as a guard rule makes the 32 read larger than the rule set it covers.

Demonstrated inside this very campaign: entry 30, "F-56: tar operands stop being read relative to -C", is KILLED -- a perfect score on a rule that VERDICT-F-56 and VERDICT-F-62 show is bypassable by five different orderings of the same command. A catalogue enumerated from fixes can only ever certify that each fix is watched; it is structurally incapable of reporting that a fix is wrong, and a 32-of-32 headline invites the reader to draw the stronger conclusion.

root_cause.mechanism: The mutant list is derived from the findings that were fixed, so a rule that was never a finding -- and, more sharply, a rule already MEASURED as unwatched in a code-enumerated campaign -- cannot appear as a survivor.

findings.title: The "class that did not exist before" is two of three, not three: the catalogue's third call-site mutant shares its anchor line with H3 and produces H3's behaviour with an unused call bolted on
evidence: CHANGELOG.md 0.75.0: "it carries a class that did not exist before: mutants that delete a **call site** while leaving the code correct", and eval/README.md repeats it. Three catalogue entries are labelled F-57 and presented as that class.

Two are genuine call-site deletions. `F-57: the bytecode sweep's only call site is deleted` removes `                _drop_bytecode(scratch)
` (src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:574) and leaves the function body intact. `F-57: the UTF-8 stderr pin is never called by the bash guard` turns `def main() -> int:
    utf8_stderr()
` into `def main() -> int:
`.

The third is not. `F-57: the run's UTC date is computed and then not used` mutates `    today = today or run_date(facts)` into `    run_date(facts)\n    today = today or date.today()`. Catalogue entry H3, `F-54: back to the machine's local calendar`, mutates the SAME line into `    today = today or date.today()`. The two differ only by a call whose result is discarded; the behaviour they produce is identical, so whatever kills H3 kills this one for the same reason.

Confirmed structurally: `eval/pinned_mutants.json` has exactly three pairs of entries sharing a `(path, old)` anchor -- H1/H2, H3/this one, and the F-56 pair -- and only this pair claims to be a different class.

Cost of the error: the release's headline story is that body mutants and call-site mutants are different claims. It is right, and the evidence offered for it is three examples of which one is a body mutant in call-site clothing.

findings.title: On macOS none of the four tar rules can fire on a binary that can perform the attack: `/usr/bin/tar` is bsdtar and rejects `--remove-files` outright, while GNU tar is installed as `gtar`, which the guard's dispatcher does not recognise
evidence: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:659 -- `elif head == "tar":`, an exact basename match. Measured: `gtar -cf <scr>/x.tar --remove-files <checkout>/hooks` -> guard rc=0 ALLOW; the same command spelled `tar` -> rc=2 DENY. `bsdtar` and the absolute path `/opt/homebrew/bin/gtar` are likewise rc=0.

And the guarded spelling cannot do the thing: `/usr/bin/tar` is a symlink to `bsdtar` (libarchive 3.7.4), and `tar -cf x.tar --remove-files hooks` prints `tar: Option --remove-files is not supported` and leaves the directory in place. So on this platform the rules that VERDICT-F-42, F-49, F-56 and F-59 built are unreachable on `tar` and unarmed on `gtar`.

Not a general aliasing complaint -- I checked which of the g-prefixed GNU tools actually exist here: `gtar` is present at /opt/homebrew/bin/gtar (GNU tar 1.35); `grm`, `gcp`, `gmv`, `gsed`, `gfind`, `gawk` are all absent. gtar is the single case, and it is the one that matters, because it is the only tar on this machine with `--remove-files`.
Scope stated: on Linux and in CI `tar` IS GNU tar, so the rules do fire there. This is a macOS-only gap -- on the platform the release's own VERDICT-F-55 fix was about.

findings.title: The pin check reads any non-zero exit as a kill, so a mutant that breaks collection instead of failing a test would be counted as defended -- the exact reading run 11 recorded a lesson about one release earlier
evidence: eval/pin_check.py:188-192 -- `result = run_suite(env)` then `if result.returncode != 0: print(... KILLED ...)`. No summary is parsed. pytest exits non-zero for a usage error (4), a collection/internal error (2 or 3) and "no tests ran" (5) as well as for a failure (1).

`.qa/lessons.md`, 2026-09-03 (run 11): "`rc != 0` also means 'usage error', 'no such file', 'collection error'; only a parsed summary tells those apart from a kill." The control run at :171-176 does assert the tree is green before the campaign, which is the other half of that lesson and is present -- but it runs once, so it cannot say what any individual mutant's non-zero exit meant.

Currently latent, and I checked rather than assumed: applied all 32 catalogue mutants in memory and `ast.parse`d the result -- 32 of 32 still parse, and every anchor matches exactly once. So no entry in today's catalogue can produce a false kill. The gap is that nothing stops the next one from doing so.

Held honestly: `probable`, not `proven`. I read the code path and established the catalogue does not currently trip it; I did not run a syntax-breaking mutant through the tool to watch it print KILLED. Doing that -- one entry, one suite run -- would settle it either way.
